items.title: Hockey Finally Has the Great Books It Deserves
items.summary: Pity the Canadian book reviewer in the autumn of 1980. An American publisher has announced, with some fanfare, a forthcoming title about the national pastime—the Canadian national pastime. Amazons: An Intimate Memoir by the First Woman Ever to Play in the National Hockey League promises to tell the story of Cleo Birdwell’s debut season with the New York Rangers. Of course, as a Canadian in good standing, you know that no woman has ever played in the NHL; there is no Cleo Birdwell. But the people behind the book are committed to the bit. At the Canadian Booksellers Association convention, held that summer in Toronto, a leggy model impersonated Birdwell, signing advance copies in a Rangers jersey. “She’s tough and sexy,” the book’s publisher whispered to a Globe and Mail reporter. Clearly this book demands attention. Perhaps the charade might even provide a welcome distraction after Canada’s rather unmiraculous sixth-place finish at Lake Placid. But what awaits within its pages confounds. The on-ice action is overshadowed by ever more elaborate accounts of Birdwell’s sexual adventures. In the course of one season, she sleeps with the Rangers’ head coach, the Rangers’ general manager, a former Rangers player, and one very jet-lagged tennis star. This is an incomplete list. In the brutal assessment of one critic in Calgary, Amazons is “little more than hardcover softcore porn that will disappoint hockey fans and heavy breathers alike.” But Amazons wasn’t smut, or not exactly. Its author was Don DeLillo. His publisher took pains to guard this secret, but there was no disguising his writing from those who already admired it. Colin McEnroe , reviewing the book for the Hartford Courant , seems to have been the first to identify DeLillo’s authorship in print. “ ‘Amazons’ is not only his book,” he wrote. “It’s his best book.” DeLillo did not share this appraisal. Although the book sold well—better, in fact, than any of his previous novels—he would not allow it to be republished. Even after the breakout success of White Noise in 1985, it never appeared in his official bibliography. Amazons soon faded into obscurity. I first learned of its existence in 2006, when the writer Keith Gessen published an essay in The New York Times Book Review titled “ In Search of the Great American Hockey Novel .” Gessen wrote of his dismay that hockey had not produced a literature as rich as that of boxing or baseball. “Where is the Chekhov of the Chicago Blackhawks?” he asked. “Who is the Stendhal of the stick to the groin?” On the shelf dedicated to immortal hockey books, Gessen placed just two volumes: Ken Dryden’s melancholy 1983 memoir, The Game , about his final season with the dynastic Montreal Canadiens, and DeLillo’s Amazons . Hockey and literature were two pursuits struggling to find an audience; perhaps, Gessen ventured, they could help each other. “What is needed now, for the sake of both hockey and literature, is more hockey literature,” he wrote. “Not just books about hockey, like ‘The Game,’ but also books not about hockey, like ‘Amazons’—which is not about hockey in just the right way.” Gessen may have been only half serious, but two decades after his essay appeared, something like his modest proposal has come to pass. The Intangibles , a new memoir by the New Yorker staff writer Nick Paumgarten, is a worthy successor to The Game , no less so for describing a career played in bruising beer leagues. The success of Heated Rivalry on HBO Max has made Rachel Reid’s queer-romance series, from which it was adapted, into a publishing juggernaut. Hockey erotica, once a fringe category, has become a cottage industry. Following that unlikely turn of events—and a January story in the Times positing DeLillo as the genre’s unlikely inventor—his editor and agent entreated him to allow Amazons back into print. DeLillo acquiesced. After 46 years, Cleo Birdwell is finally making her curtain call. A mazons was not DeLillo’s first foray into the world of sport. That distinction belongs to End Zone , his heady 1972 novel about college football and the madness of mutual assured destruction. Later, in the prologue to Underworld (1997), he turned to baseball, with his panoramic account of Bobby Thomson’s “shot heard ’round the world.” In those pages, too, nuclear war hangs in the air; the White House announced on the same day in 1951 that the Soviet Union had conducted a bomb test. The tone of Amazons is zanier, more absurd, untroubled by nuclear annihilation. If anything hangs in the air, it’s the reek of the hockey bag. Cleo Birdwell is the pride of Badger, Ohio, which she describes as a small, straightforward town where “the school was on School Street, the bank was on Bank Street, the river ran by River Road.” But Cleo is not an ingenue; she’s a hockey player. No amount of towel snapping or jock talk seems capable of making her blush. On the contrary, she’s a wry raconteur of her teammates’ puerile antics. One player, Eric Torkleson, has such an enormous member that it becomes an honorary Ranger, known as Torkle. “A player would say, ‘How’s Torkle doing today?’ Or, ‘Who’s playing Torkle in the movie version?’ Or, ‘Is it true Torkle’s being asked to endorse Jimmy Carter?’ ” The book is as sex-drenched as the Calgary reviewer warned. But sex functions less as titillation and more as the engine of the satire. Its object, mostly, is the American male. Cleo is frank, confident, liberated; her lovers are neurotic and narcissistic. One, the Rangers’ general manager, is unable to perform after Cleo makes an offhanded Watergate joke. How could he, having been reminded of this great blow to the male ego? “We lost our manhood, our sense of pride and honor, our belief in God and Dick Nixon, our deepest dreams, hopes, and ambitions.” (In an earlier scene, the GM has been deflated by intrusive thoughts of Torkle.) Men who aren’t trying to sleep with Cleo are usually trying to persuade her to sell something—the rank commercialization of sport is one of the novel’s many prescient targets. Cleo is asked to hawk a sensual whirlpool bath called the Primal Vortex and a snack food called Amazons, especially formulated for “every age, every size, every make of woman.” She refuses both endorsements. In the middle of the Rangers’ season, Hughes Tool, the conglomerate that owns the team, hires a Saudi national to run it, hoping to push through a business deal with “men in the Gulf.” DeLillo seems to have anticipated our age of sportswashing, too. To be clear, Amazons is not a lost masterpiece. Some scenes drag, like runaway SNL sketches. The dialogue, although generally hilarious, can take on a rim-shot quality, as if DeLillo were doing Dangerfield. A sportswriter confesses to Cleo that his ex-wife is now a lesbian. “Who is she a lesbian with?” she asks. “Paine, Webber, Jackson and Curtis. She’s a financial analyst.” Robert Gottlieb, DeLillo’s editor at the time, turned down Amazons . You wonder how the man who convinced Joseph Heller that Catch‑22 sounded funnier than Catch‑18 might have sharpened this manuscript. [ From the May 1973 issue: “The Bucky Wunderlick Story,” by Don DeLillo ] As for the hockey quotient, some fans may wish that DeLillo had set more of the novel between the boards. But Amazons is like Dickie Dunn’s newspaper accounts of the Charlestown Chiefs in Slap Shot : It captures the spirit of the thing. The locker-room banter, at once clever and cretinous; the relentless travel to frozen, past-their-prime cities; the vicious play of the Philadelphia Flyers and the bloodlust of their fans (“screaming made-up and never-before-heard obscenities, as though they were overwhelmed by a massive thyroid deficiency”); the otherworldly allure of a sport conducted, improbably, on a sheet of ice. “In a way it is the most romantic game,” the Rangers’ head coach, Jean-Paul Larousse, says. “There is a lightness, a speed without effort. It is the skates.” It was lightness and speed that drew Nick Paumgarte

items.title: What If the Apocalypse Is Already Here?
items.summary: On a patch of ground in the City of London, the exact site of the former East India Company’s headquarters, stands a puzzling structure with the nickname the “ Inside-Out Building .” Unlike the glittering, knifelike high-rises that surround it, the edifice is covered in a shell of equipment: all of the air ducts, electrical lines, elevators, and pipes run up the exterior. Inside, Lloyd’s of London, the three-century-old powerhouse firm, props up the globe’s insurers and guarantees financial security. So when a race of amorphous beings called the iGhetti arrives in England, Lloyd’s seems like a logical target. There is no better way to dominate humanity than to take over the economic heart of the empire. And there might be no better place for M. John Harrison to situate his new, Booker Prize–shortlisted novel, The End of Everything , than a building of great significance that is also irresistibly weird. The End of Everything is brief and confounding; it also doesn’t care a whit for the conventions of dystopian fiction. It’s set about 20 or 30 years in the future, mostly in the small coastal towns of Kent, where strange entities (they might be aliens, or bio-machines, or really anything) wash up onshore. The “artefacts,” as they are called, arrived around the same time as the iGhetti; together they somehow upended life as everyone knew it, rendering Britain unrecognizable within a decade. As one man, Phillip Tennent, moves through this uncanny new world order, all of the tropes of postapocalyptic fiction fall away in favor of a far more timely and provocative proposal: The apocalypse might not be an end at all, but simply a long chain of baffling, disorienting incidents. Writers have been thinking about different versions of doomsday for thousands of years—the tale of Noah’s ark is just one example of an ancient religious story about the eradication of humanity. But the fear that seems to plague modern minds is that it might all end with a whimper, rather than a bang. Through rants about late-stage capitalism , that infamous dog-in-a-fire meme , and other expressions of alarm, it’s become more and more common to hear people worrying—or joking—that the world is enduring a rolling apocalypse, a series of catastrophes so slow-moving that they won’t prevent you from browsing a J.Crew sale while everything falls apart. Because fiction favors drama, most postapocalyptic novels are structured around a single Event. In Emily St. John Mandel’s Station Eleven , Stephen King’s The Stand , and Ling Ma’s Severance , it’s a population-decimating plague; in Cormac McCarthy ’s The Road and Walter M. Miller Jr.’s A Canticle for Leibowitz , it seems to be a nuclear explosion; in Octavia Butler’s Parable of the Sower and Claire Vaye Watkins’s Gold Fame Citrus , it’s rapid, unstoppable climate collapse. Whatever the Event may be, it kicks off a transformation in how people live. Bands of survivors poke around for degrading tins of food, tribes form and fight, the remnants of modern life waste away under coats of dust and piles of rubble. There is an immovable sense of a before and an after—distinct time periods that cannot be reconciled. Harrison, however, favors inscrutability. He doesn’t make his Event an act of decimation; society keeps on going even as social structures dissolve. Characters still eat croissants, argue about World War II battles, and throw dance parties despite what they term “the disaster.” Tennent, who lives by the sea, discovers an artefact and plans to sell it. Over time, as he watches the artefact morph (it grows hands and eventually speaks), he repeatedly wonders why his country keeps changing—and how. No matter which way he turns his mind, the particulars of what has happened to Britain never resolve, as in an eye test in which each flick of the optometrist’s machinery reveals only a different kind of fuzziness. [ Read: Apocalypse, constantly ] Some facts are laid out: Europe has disappeared (one confused character makes a sign that aptly asks, HOW CAN YOU MISPLACE A CONTINENT? ); migration has reversed course and airplanes no longer fly, so Britons regularly board ferries departing for other lands. The idea of an economy is now a historical notion, and there is no government to speak of, so militias patrol the towns, but only off the page. Londoners fled the dangerous, iGhetti-occupied city, but then returned, despite the fact that the British military continued to bombard the Lloyd’s building. (Violence is a hallmark of the postapocalyptic novel, but Harrison’s characters kill with a paucity of forethought that makes McCarthy’s rogues seem like Montessori teachers by comparison.) Most facts, however, are disputed, and even the idea of a “fact” seems to have collapsed. The iGhetti might have “come out of the internet,” or they may embody “a re-enchantment of the world.” They could be aliens, or AI, or spiritual visitors. Harrison once calls them “tall writhing bursts of light” but otherwise avoids describing them as corporeal, as if they are some galactic version of Catholicism’s Holy Spirit. The term bad patch is used to describe a plot of land that’s been taken over by the iGhetti—such as the Lloyd’s building—but it is also an all-purpose term for someone who can’t see their way through the never-ending tumult. “Using the phrase in its older, pre-crisis sense,” Harrison writes, “the way you might talk about a failed marriage or career—was perhaps an unconscious attempt to normalise the inexplicable and minimise the disaster.” But what was the disaster? All Harrison will say is that there was “a decade of confusion,” and “by the time things came back into focus, the climate had changed. Geography had changed.” Nobody can even agree on whether the iGhetti are an external phenomenon or something humanity has brought upon itself. Perhaps unsurprising, all of this is a metaphor for the condition of England today . It’s no coincidence that the novel is set near Hastings, the site of the famous 1066 battle that created the modern English nation, and that the iGhetti commandeer a financial quarter that has been hollowed out by Brexit. [ Read: How Britain became as poor as Mississippi ] Yet the subject of Harrison’s experiment is larger than one referendum on territorial boundaries—or any single Event at all. He seems to be asking how humans will respond when they discover, en masse, that they are no longer in control of the planet’s destiny. Really, The End of Everything is a novel about surrender. “The apocalypse,” one character writes, “seemed to withhold itself, quickly becoming just another historical continuity. That is to say, we got used to it. No one had expected the utter banality of that.” Harrison’s sociological portrait is attuned to the common idea that disaster can quickly become boring—or all too quickly assimilated and ignored. Horrible images of global catastrophe—razed cities, drowned villages—now flit through our phones in between makeup tutorials and political punditry. Pondering barbarity or devastation is as easy as pondering a lunch menu. So what might people do if the tide turns against the whole of humanity, if the End Times finally come? In Harrison’s estimation, they’ll shrug. As bleak as this interpretation may sound, the novel is expansive rather than dismissive. It reaches out for connection, feeling at once bizarrely creative and, on a psychological level, strikingly familiar. In a short novel, in a wholly original way, Harrison has managed to sketch not just a world, but a worldview. I suspect that he knew he needed to create a new style of language and imagery to convey the emotional reality of a world “disconnected from itself.” As John Ashbery put it in 1977, “You can’t say it that way any more.” The same is true now.

items.title: The Crisis of Masculinity Is Actually a Crisis of Capitalism
items.summary: In September, a former Cornell student sued the university and seven fraternity members , who she says drugged and raped her. Nobody was arrested; only two were expelled. According to her lawyer, some of the others were allowed to make up for it by writing an essay . All of which is to say: I understand why the phrase “male loneliness epidemic” makes women want to gouge their eyes out. And still, I’m curious. Men are a lifelong academic fascination of mine. Also, they control everything, so if they’ve all gone off the deep end, I’d like to know. Or, as Luke Kennard puts it in his brilliant Booker shortlisted comic novel Black Bag : “When damaged men have money and influence, that’s a problem for the whole world.” The book’s jacket calls it “an investigation into the crisis of masculinity.” The Sunday Times found it a meditation on how hard it is to be a man right now . One blurb sells it as “comic relief” from the manosphere, while another says it takes aim at “modern-day masculinity.” Even the Booker judges predicted we’d all be discussing what it says about modern men. I was interested. And then, I read Black Bag . It’s about a guy who can’t make his rent. The narrator is an unnamed 37-year-old London actor. On the first few pages, we learn that he hasn’t had a paid job in months. He’s behind on rent and most of his utility bills. In his words: “I have measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford.” Desperate for work, he answers an ad. A university professor, Dr. Blend, needs an actor to sit silently at the back of his lectures for a term, zipped into a black leather bag. It’s absurd and demeaning. It also gives our protagonist, for a few months, “a level of fiscal security I have never experienced in adult life.” He resolves to do a good job. He’s thrilled. Almost immediately, it’s more than just a job to him. On his days off, he still zips himself back into his bag and shuffles around London. Soon he’s wearing the bag on the bus, in cafés, everywhere. “I would just as soon be black bag than whatever my self is,” he says. “What am I without black bag? Without black bag I am some pitiful and unremarkable man going around, doing things. Shameful.” When our narrator is zipped into his bag in the lectures, mind free to wander, he doesn’t imagine a life of fame, fortune, or comically large biceps, even though he is both an actor and a man. He plays out soft, slow fantasies of life in an isolated Swedish town where he works in the sawmill, where “my superiors would be supportive and gently amused as I learned the ropes.” His wildest escapist fantasy is having a decent boss. Kennard gives his narrator a job so stupid, and a subsequent sense of self so powerful, that the book becomes a masterful exploration of the dignity of showing up to work. Black Bag is more than a discourse on our forlorn men. It’s the most pro-labor novel of the year. And yet, it’s been pegged as a “masculinity novel.” To be fair, the book is about a lonely man. Kennard writes beautifully of his protagonist’s isolation and struggle to communicate with those around him. As he says, regarding his parents: “What I want to say is thank you. English people have such a deep-seated suspicion of disingenuousness that we often forego gratitude altogether. It is feasible to go your entire life without ever expressing a single emotion just in case you didn’t mean it.” The man is lonely. Black Bag is more than a discourse on our forlorn men. It’s the most pro-labor novel of the year. But I wonder if there’s a marketing element, too: Male loneliness is so in right now. “The crisis of masculinity” is fresh and buzzy; “the crisis of rent” is old and dull. It’s more fun to talk about men being all messed up than it is to talk about oligarchy. But I worry that trying to disguise a crisis of capitalism with a crisis of masculinity plays into the hands of those same oligarchs. If we’re going to talk about what men need, we can’t avoid what’s currently on offer. I’m not British, I’m not a man, I’m not an actor, and I have no interest in wearing a black leather bag, professionally or otherwise. But I live in America, where “masculinity,” as a political conversation, has curdled. MAGA’s plan for men is gender essentialism: Everyone else gets smaller so men have room to be “men” again. JD Vance wants to $9,000 per child , married couples only . The Heritage Foundation has asked RFK Jr. to go after the birth control pill , on the grounds that estrogen in the water is making male fish girly and also potentially doing something to our boys (???). Josh Hawley’s solution for men—laid forth in his painful book, Manhood —prescribes Bible study, early marriage, and absolutely NO porn or video games. Neither!! In the words of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth: “We are leaving wokeness and weakness behind. No more pronouns. No more climate change obsession. No more emergency vaccine mandates. No more dudes in dresses, we’re done with that shit.” The through-line is that masculinity is a fixed quantity. Bad actors—women, Democrats, trans kids, immigrants, feminists, Rosie O’Donnell, etc—have been siphoning it off, and the true patriots need to wrestle it back. Very few of my needs are specific to my gender. The whole premise is not merely offensive, but also misguided. My issue is twofold. First: The assumption that men’s needs are about their manhood. I don’t know what it’s like to be a man, but I do know what it’s like to be a woman. Very few of my needs are specific to my gender. I need food. I need health insurance. I need affordable housing. I need my daughter’s daycare to stop making up fake holidays to cancel school (no offense). And sure, I occasionally need a tampon. But if I had to pick between health insurance and tampons, I’d go with health insurance. I can always just wear black jeans, or better yet, a black leather bag. I don’t mean to suggest that different constituencies don’t have different needs, but boiling a person’s needs down to only their demographics disguises far more universal economic problems. Second—and more importantly—these “masculinity” solutions shift the onus away from the people in power and onto the individuals. Sorry, guys, we don’t have policy solutions for you because we can’t raise taxes on our rich friends, but have you ever considered marrying younger? Praying more? Keeping your wife at home so she doesn’t outshine you? Having kids? Quitting porn? Getting your testosterone checked? Kennard’s narrator, by contrast, tries none of these. What’s missing from his life isn’t “manhood,” it’s a stable and fulfilling source of income. And the numbers would suggest he’s not alone. In 1983, one in four working men belonged to a union. Today it’s one in ten. By 2010, NAFTA had cost the US nearly 700,000 jobs, according to the Economic Policy Institute, most of them in manufacturing: a field that’s 71 percent male. In response, Trump did NAFTA 2.0, plus a plethora of tariffs that nobody expected to bring the factories back. And the next version of government-sponsored job losses (AI) is likely to be even more widespread. Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently told Axios that AI could push unemployment as high as 20 percent, and then went back to building it. And still, we’ve seen no federal AI regulation. We’re living in a world in which a good job and reliable income are increasingly out of reach. Or, as our narrator says: “a life of quiet desperation is an impossible dream for my generation . . . We’d love nothing more than affordable accommodation to fail in.” This affects everyone, but men fall under the umbrella of “everyone.” I don’t mean to suggest that men are more vulnerable to a bad economy than anyone else (all evidence would suggest the opposite). items.title: 7 Books That Weigh the Choice of Motherhood
items.summary: When I began trying to get pregnant, I didn’t know exactly why I wanted to have a child, but I knew my parents had something to do with the desire. Not directly: They never told me I should have children and would never have pressured me into making a decision either way. I felt their influence in terms of heritage. How did my parents’ choice to become parents—and my perceived effect of that choice on their lives—seep into my decision making? How did the African-American, Jamaican, Lebanese, and Haitian cultures they grew up in influence their decision and mine? Even though the choice to have children is often framed as one that involves one or two people, this ignores the truth that families and cultures often influence the decision. I wanted to explore this in my multigenerational novel, The Meaning of Daughter . I started with the first-generation character, Merjan, a woman who wants to dedicate herself completely to her art, even though her family and her Lebanese-Haitian community expect her to be solely a wife and mother. I traced how immigration, cultural values, and personal ambition influenced what she thought about having children. My curiosity about the effects of her choices around motherhood led me through the lives of her daughter and her daughter’s daughter, spanning seven decades and three countries. The authors of the novels on this list have shown me that there are many variations to the questions I grappled with in my novel about what goes into reproductive decisions. Whether it’s by showing how the death of a parent can shape the meaning of becoming a parent, or how cultural conflicts between a parent and child raised in different countries can manifest in conversations about having children, each author adds a complex layer to the discussion. Still Born by Guadalupe Nettel, translated by Rosalind Harvey Still Born ties together two stories: one that begins with the narrator’s decision not to have children, and one that centers on her friend’s decision to try to get pregnant. Early in the novel, the narrator has a conversation with her mother about her choice to get her tubes tied. At first it seems her mother is upset, but she ends up being more understanding than the narrator had expected. However, her mother can’t help but add, “It’s important to have someone to love, someone to take care of. It makes us less selfish.” The protagonist takes this to heart, as the novel redefines motherhood to include the narrator’s care of her community. She discovers the pleasures and meaning of caring for her friend who is struggling to support a baby with severe disabilities, her neighbor who is recovering from an abusive relationship, and her neighbor’s young son. Burnt Sugar by Avni Doshi The first part of Burnt Sugar takes the reader through a thicket of history and emotions surrounding a complicated mother-daughter relationship. The protagonist must find a way to be at peace with caring for her mother, who has dementia, despite her history of abandonment by her mother as a child. When, two-thirds of the way into the novel, the protagonist decides to have a baby, her relationship with her mother is framed in a new light. For this protagonist, having a baby takes the form of revenge against her mother, and serves as a way to start a mother-child relationship free from the burdens of the past. The book’s gothic ending speaks to the paradox of this complex desire, and the power of intergenerational trauma to shape a family’s course despite the intentions to escape it. Cold Enough for Snow by Jessica Au On its surface, this novel is about one woman’s trip to Japan with her mother. They walk around Tokyo taking photographs, visiting art museums, and eating in restaurants. Slowly and subtly, the narrative drama reveals itself: The narrator is contemplating whether or not to have children. She weighs the private self—her thoughts, observations, and attraction to beauty and wonder—against the communal self that cares for others. At one point in the novel, the narrator’s mother says to the narrator that when she was growing up, “[her mother] had never thought of herself in isolation, but rather as inextricably linked to others.” This proves to be an important focal point of the novel, as the narrator continues on a solo portion of the journey, leaving the reader doubting whether the narrator’s mother was ever really on the trip. Alone and frightened on a hike that has gone on too long, she considers what she has inherited from her mother, and her inability to distinguish where her mother ends and she begins. One Leg on Earth by ‘Pemi Aguda In the Lagos of One Leg on Earth , pregnant women are drowning themselves en masse, seemingly drawn to the water by a supernatural force. After finding herself unexpectedly pregnant, the protagonist of the novel must grapple with her desire to continue the pregnancy despite the danger it brings into her life. When faced with one of her friend’s criticism of her choice to keep her baby, Yosoye thinks about the chance to cultivate the type of intimacy she never had with her own mother, “Could someone with a mother like that understand what a child might mean for Yosoye? Yosoye who’d never even had her mother to call her own?” Aguda is adept at showing both the draw and the sense of danger inherent in motherhood, as she paints a rich landscape of pregnancy as a psychological, social, and artistic force. Breasts and Eggs by Mieko Kawakami, translated by Sam Bett and David Boyd The heart of this novel lies in a complicated desire shared by two sisters, Natsuko and Makiko, who both want to exert control over their bodies in ways that don’t make sense to the other. In the first section of the novel, Natsuko, the narrator, hosts Makiko and Makiko’s daughter in her apartment in Tokyo, as Makiko looks into getting breast implants. Natsuko doesn’t understand Makiko’s obsession with changing her breasts and doesn’t make an effort to understand what’s driving her sister either. In the novel’s second section, the tables are turned. Natsuko wants to try to have a child on her own. Makiko wonders why Natsuko would choose to be a single mother—knowing from Makiko’s life as well as their shared childhood—how hard it can be. Natsuko ends up turning to friends, colleagues, and other people in her community to help her understand her desire to have a child. The novel not only explores the power of women fully owning their bodily desires, but also the psychic pain of not truly being accepted on your own terms by those closest to you. Red at the Bone Jacqueline Woodson What Is a Mother Allowed to Write? Part of me believes that as a mother I’m committing some sin of impropriety by writing the ugliest parts of my life --> Part of me believes that as a mother I’m committing some sin of impropriety by writing the ugliest parts of my life Oct 2 – Katie Bennett Craft Red at the Bone explores the impacts of an unexpected teen pregnancy, focusing not just on the young father and mother, but their parents too. Through the novel’s first-person rotating point of view, Woodson is able to jump backwards and forwards in time, and we see the teen couple’s parents both as parents—worried about how the pregnancy will affect their children’s futures—and as grandparents, who couldn’t imagine wishing their granddaughter had never been conceived. Through these jumps in time we can also see how the young couple’s respective relationships with their parents affected their desire for intimacy with their daughter once she was born. The novel’s expansive gaze does not shy away from the wounding emotions that can accompany an unexpected pregnancy, as well as the potential for these wounds to change over time. items.title: Ask Ethan: Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth?
items.summary: One of the great quests in all of science is to discover, at a fundamental level, what the Universe is actually made of. If you took every amount of matter and energy that existed — or even could exist — and cut it up into its smallest possible chunks, until only something that was uncuttable was left, you’d be left with the fundamental, elementary particles that composed our Universe. In physics, this took us first down to the level of the atom, then to atomic nuclei and electrons, then to protons, neutrons, and electrons, and finally to our modern Standard Model of elementary particles: complete with quarks, charged leptons, neutrinos, their antimatter counterparts, the gluons, the photon, the W-and-Z bosons, and one additional unique particle, the Higgs boson. Of all of those particles, the Higgs boson is the most recently discovered particle: found only at particle accelerators, like the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, in 2012. But what’s the story of the Higgs boson? What makes it so unique, where does it come from, and how does it fit in with everything else that we know? That’s what Vu H Nguyen wants to know, asking: “Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth? [It is] difficult for me to understand, but I think this is very important in particle physics. Maybe you can explain it in an easier way?” When we think about matter, we normally think about “fundamental” in the way we outlined above: by cutting it up into its smallest indivisible component parts. But there’s more to the story, and the Higgs boson requires us to go deeper than any other known particle in order to understand it. Here’s the story. From macroscopic scales down to subatomic ones, the sizes of the fundamental particles play only a small role in determining the sizes of composite structures. Whether the building blocks are truly fundamental and/or point-like particles is still not known, but we do understand the Universe from large, cosmic scales down to tiny, subatomic ones. The scale of electrons, quarks, and gluons is the limit to how far we’ve ever probed nature: down to scales of ~10^-19 meters, where these structures remain point-like. Credit : Magdalena Kowalska/CERN/ISOLDE team Here in our Universe, we’re mostly familiar with the particles that are common and stable today: atoms and the subatomic particles they’re composed of. Atoms are made of electrons that orbit the atomic nucleus, which in turn is made of protons and neutrons, which themselves are made of quarks and gluons. If you want to see what types of quarks are in there, however, you have to collide particles together. You have to collide them hard enough to break inside the atom, to crack open the atomic nucleus, to split apart the individual protons and neutrons, and to smash them directly into individual elementary particles. When you do that, you discover something amazing. You don’t just reveal what these composite structures inside the atom are made of, you also gain the ability to create brand new particles, including heavy, unstable, short-lived particles. Through the power of colliders, we don’t just make electrons and the up-and-down quarks that compose protons and neutrons, but also: muons and taus, the heavier cousins of electrons, positrons, antimuons, and antitaus, the antimatter counterparts of those charged leptons, strange, charm, bottom, and top quarks, the antimatter counterparts of all six flavors of quarks (the antiquarks), photons, gluons, and W-and-Z bosons, which are the gauge bosons, and the Higgs boson as well. These, along with the neutrinos and antineutrinos (which can’t be directly observed in colliders, but can be observed through other means), make up all of the known elementary particles, and the entirety of the Standard Model of elementary particles. This diagram of the Standard Model particles shows the fermions in the top row, the gauge bosons in the middle row, and the Higgs on the bottom. The lines indicate couplings, and you can see which fermionic particles couple to which of the forces by the blue lines. Everything with mass couples to the Higgs; the only particles which are massless (and hence, do not) are the photon and the gluons. The theoretical graviton, not shown here, couples to everything with energy: all particles and antiparticles. If there are new particles out there, their couplings may reveal their presence, indirectly, through precision measurements that compare the particles’ observed properties with those predicted by the Standard Model. Credit : TriTertButoxy/Stannered at English Wikipedia We can measure all sorts of properties about these particles from our collider-detector experiments. In particular, we can, by creating enough of them and building detectors around the collision points where those particles come into existence — created from energy via Einstein’s E = mc as long as all of the necessary quantum properties like energy, momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, and so on are conserved — measure all sorts of properties associated with them. We can determine: their rest masses, their electric charges, their intrinsic angular momenta (i.e., their spin), their mean lifetimes, their weak hypercharge and weak isospin, their possible decay products (all of the different pathways through which the unstable ones can decay), and their branching ratios (the rate at which they decay through their various pathways), chief among them. The Standard Model isn’t just about the particles that exist, but about their key relationships and properties. The quarks and leptons make up what we conventionally know of as “matter” (while the antiquarks and antileptons make up “antimatter”), but the gauge bosons determine how they interact with one another. We normally talk about this as the four fundamental forces, as particles and antiparticles interact through gravity (which we don’t know whether it’s quantum in nature; it’s outside of the Standard Model), electromagnetism (mediated by the photon), the weak nuclear force (mediated by the W-and-Z bosons), and the strong nuclear force (mediated by the gluons). Sure, there are still mysteries that we have that the Standard Model can’t explain: gravity, the values for the rest masses of the particles, the abundance of matter over antimatter in the Universe, and the existence of dark matter and dark energy among them. But for what the Standard Model does give us, it’s an incredibly powerful description of reality. The rest masses of the fundamental particles in the Universe determine when and under what conditions they can be created, and also relate to how long they can survive after their creation during the hot Big Bang. The more massive a particle is, the less time it can spontaneously be created in the early Universe, and the shorter its lifetime will be. Although we can explain particle masses through a coupling to the Higgs, we have no way of successfully predicting their values; they must be experimentally measured in order to be determined. Credit : Universe-review So where does the Higgs boson come from? In order to answer that, we can’t start here in our Universe today, nor can we even start with the “little bangs” we create in our particle colliders here on Earth. Instead, we have to go all the way back to the hot Big Bang, where higher energies and hotter temperatures were achieved than in anything we can create here on Earth. Back then, we still had the quarks and leptons (and antiquarks and antileptons) that we have today, as well as the gluons. They all still needed energy in order to exist, but they didn’t possess the rest masses that they have today. items.title: Life is the most important problem in physics
items.summary: Descartes cut open living dogs and insisted their cries were just the noises of a machine. Astrophysicist and astrobiologist Adam Frank, a professor at the University of Rochester and author of The Little Book of Aliens, argues that the same life-as-machine metaphor still shapes how we think about AI, and that it gets life fundamentally wrong. Living things are self-creating, self-repairing systems that decide what matters to them, which is why he calls today’s AI an artificial mimic rather than an intelligence. This video Life is the most important problem in physics is featured on Big Think .
